question: What should you check or do first when a patient is brought in with a suspected poisoning?

options.D: Stabilizing the airway, breathing, and circulation

explanation: Great nursing rule to keep in mind! ABC comes before anything else in an emergency. We have to make sure our patient is breathing and has a steady heartbeat before we worry about testing or finding out what they swallowed.

question: Why do we wait to find out the exact name of the poison instead of panicking right away?

options.A: Laboratory tests are always inaccurate in the first hour
options.B: Immediate life threats must be managed to prevent death
options.C: Hospital policy forbids asking family members about pill bottles
options.D: The poison usually breaks down and cannot be identified later

explanation: Spot on! If a patient's airway is blocked or their heart stops, knowing the chemical name of the poison won't save them. We stabilize life first, investigate second.

question: A patient has overdosed on an opioid. Which signs would you expect to see on assessment?

options.A: High fever and dry, flushed skin
options.D: Rapid heart rate and dilated pupils

explanation: You've got this! Opioids slow down the nervous system. That means they make breathing dangerously slow and cause the pupils to shrink down to tiny 'pinpoints'.

question: Your patient has dry skin, blurry vision, can't pass urine, and seems quite confused after taking an unknown drug. What toxidrome are they showing?
explanation: Think of anticholinergic drugs as drying up all the body's moisture—hence the dry skin, urinary retention, and blurry vision, plus a confused mind!

question: Which substance is often given early to trap toxins in the stomach before they get into the bloodstream?
explanation: Activated charcoal works like a magnet! It grabs onto many drugs and chemicals right in the gut so they can't get absorbed into the body.

question: Why don't we use syrup of ipecac anymore to treat poisoning?

options.A: It is too expensive to manufacture
options.B: It causes unpredictable vomiting and risks aspiration
options.C: It permanently stains the lining of the stomach
options.D: It neutralizes all known hospital antidotes

explanation: Ipecac causes vomiting at random, delayed times. If the patient vomits and breathes it into their lungs (aspiration), it can cause serious damage, so it's a no-go today.

question: What is the go-to treatment to quickly filter out dangerous levels of a heavy-duty poison like lithium?
explanation: When the kidneys just can't keep up, hemodialysis steps in to act like an artificial kidney, filtering the dangerous drug straight out of the blood.

question: A patient took a drug that leaves the body mainly through urine. As a nurse, how can you help speed up this process?

options.A: Administering prescribed intravenous fluids to promote urine output
options.B: Inserting a nasogastric tube for continuous suction
options.C: Restricting all oral and IV fluids

explanation: Hydration is key! Giving IV fluids helps the kidneys produce enough urine to safely flush water-soluble toxins out of the body.

question: Which specific antidote is given to protect the liver during a dangerous paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?
explanation: N-acetylcysteine is a lifesaver here! It replenishes a vital liver chemical (glutathione) and stops paracetamol byproducts from destroying the liver tissue.

question: How does naloxone work so quickly to reverse an opioid overdose?

options.A: By competing for and blocking opioid receptor sites
options.B: By destroying the opioid molecules in the stomach
options.C: By coating the lining of the lungs to block absorption
options.D: By stimulating the kidneys to filter out the drug faster

explanation: Think of naloxone as a master key that pushes the opioid out of the lock (the receptor) and takes its place, instantly waking up the breathing center!

question: What is the main strategy used to treat most cases of acute poisoning in the hospital?

options.C: Immediate surgical removal of the stomach

explanation: Don't stress trying to memorize an antidote for everything—most poisons don't have one! The core treatment is simply keeping vital organs working smoothly until the body clears the poison on its own.

question: A patient with a severe drug overdose suddenly starts having seizures. Which medication will the doctor likely order first?
explanation: Benzodiazepines are the go-to class for calming down an overexcited brain and stopping toxin-induced seizures safely.

question: Which of these is NOT something a nurse should do when monitoring a recovery from poisoning?

options.A: Tracking precise fluid intake and output
options.B: Discharging the patient without a psychiatric evaluation

explanation: Never skip mental health! If a patient self-harmed through poisoning, they must receive a careful psychological evaluation and support before they can safely leave the hospital.

question: Why must we keep monitoring a patient for days after a paracetamol overdose, even if they claim they feel fine?

options.A: The initial antidote causes permanent memory loss
options.B: Activated charcoal remains in the blood for a week
options.C: Delayed kidney stones always develop on the third day
options.D: Liver damage and organ failure develop progressively over time

explanation: Paracetamol is sneaky. A patient might look totally normal at first, but liver damage builds up quietly over the next few days, which is why close observation is a must.
